Dockerfile.text:
FROM node:22-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY calc.mjs server.mjs ./
RUN mkdir /data && chown node /data
USER node
ENV PORT=8080 STATE=/data/state.json
VOLUME /data
EXPOSE 8080
HEALTHCHECK CMD wget -qO- http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz || exit 1
CMD ["node", "server.mjs"]

README.md.text:
# Event Seating Chart Optimizer

Free, browser-only seating chart optimizer for weddings, banquets and events.
Paste a guest list (with optional family or party), write who should sit
together, who to keep apart and who is pinned to a table, and it assigns every
guest to a table with the most wishes met within capacity. Shows each table,
every wish it could not meet, a comparison with seating in list order, and a
CSV for place cards. Nothing is uploaded.

**Live tool:** https://duncan-haywood.github.io/monorepo-projects/event-seating-chart-optimizer/

Open `index.html`. No build step, no dependencies. `node --test` runs the suite.


## Run your own "find your table" page (self-hosted)

The browser tool seats the room; `server.mjs` gets the answer to your guests. You paste the guest list and wishes into
`/admin?key=...` and click **Seat and publish**; guests open **one link** (`/find?t=...`), type their name and see their
table number and who else sits there. Meals, groups and wishes are never shown. No accounts, no app, no third party:
zero dependencies, one JSON file on a disk you own.

- **Alternatives today:** paid wedding sites (Zola, The Knot, WithJoy) and event apps (Social Tables, AllSeated) host the
  guest list for you behind their accounts. This is only the optimise-and-look-up loop, MIT-licensed, on your box.
- **Deploy:** `docker compose up -d` with `ADMIN_KEY` and `GUEST_TOKEN` set (`openssl rand -hex 16`), `fly.toml` for Fly.io,
  or `render.yaml` for Render, each in your own account. Keep `STATE` on a persistent disk. Put it behind HTTPS.
- **Meal picks (optional):** type your choices in the admin box ("Chicken, Fish, Vegetarian"); after finding their table each guest can pick a meal, you see the tally in `/admin` and download `/admin/meals.csv` (name, table, meal) for the caterer. Republishing drops picks for guests you removed. Anyone holding the guest link can set any listed guest's meal, so share it only with guests.
- Anyone with the guest link sees every guest name; share it only with the guests. `node --test` covers it.

- `calc.mjs` - parsing, the pair-weight matrix, simulated annealing with a
  softened never-together penalty, a hill-climbing polish, the report, and an
  independent `verifyPlan` check.
- `reseat` / `parsePlanCsv` in `calc.mjs` - late RSVPs and drop-outs: paste last time's
  CSV and re-seat; each returning guest is tied to an anchor at their old table, so
  only moves worth their cost happen (stickiness low/medium/high). Pins and
  never-together rules still win.
- `tableSignsHtml` in `calc.mjs` - a print-ready page, one sheet per table (big number, guest names), opened from the "Print table signs" button.
- `floorPlanHtml` in `calc.mjs` - a print-ready floor plan, landscape, three tables across: each table is a circle with its guests around it in seat order (the order the signs and CSV use), so you see who sits next to whom. No meals shown; opened from "Print floor plan". It does not model the room itself, only the tables.
- `escortBoardHtml` in `calc.mjs` - a print-ready "find your table" list, every guest by last name with their table number, for the welcome sign or escort cards.
- `placeCardsHtml` in `calc.mjs` - folded tent place cards, 8 to a US Letter page: each guest's name upside down on the top half and the right way up with their table number below, so it reads from both sides once folded. Grouped by table, no meals shown; opened from "Print folded place cards".
- Group column and mixing: a third column (`Name | party | group`, e.g. "Bride side", "Singles", "Kids") plus a spread / cluster setting. Spread nudges each group to different tables so sides of the family mingle; cluster seats a group together. Pairs, parties and pins still win; the report shows each group's head-count per table (`groupMix`).
- Meal column and caterer sheet: a fourth column (`Name | party | group | meal`, e.g. "vegetarian") is tallied per table (`mealTally`) and shown in the report; "Print meal counts for the caterer" (`catererSheetHtml`) gives one total per meal plus a per-table grid, and the CSV gains a Meal column. Meals never appear on table signs or the find-your-table list.
- Different-sized tables: the optional box `1: 12, 5: 6` gives table 1 twelve seats and table 5 six (a head table, a kids table); every other table keeps the seats-per-table figure, fill-evenly shares what the sized tables leave, and the table count grows to fit when left blank (`parseTableSizes`, `capacitiesOf`). Capacity checks, `verifyPlan` and late-RSVP `reseat` all use each table's own size.
- Access needs: list the step-free tables in the "Accessible tables" box (`1, 2`) and add `Grandma Rose @ accessible` to the wishes (also `access`, `step-free`, `wheelchair`). That guest is only ever seated at a listed table, in the search, the polish and late-RSVP re-seats; `validateSpec` says so when no table is listed, a pin contradicts it, or the accessible tables are too small (`parseAccessTables`, `accessSeated`). Which tables are accessible is your call; the tool does not know the venue.
- Save and return: guests, wishes, settings and the last plan CSV are remembered on this device and can be saved to or loaded from a setup file, so a planner can come back as RSVPs arrive.
- `shareFragment` / `parseShareFragment` in `calc.mjs` - "Copy share link": the whole setup packed into the URL fragment (`#s=...`), so a partner or planner opens the same lists from one link. The fragment is never sent to a server; the link contains the guest names, so share it only with people who may see them.
- `importGuestSheet` in `calc.mjs` - paste rows from a spreadsheet or RSVP export (or choose a .csv): tab, comma or semicolon separated, header columns for name (or first and last), household/party, side/group, meal, RSVP and plus-one are recognised, declined RSVPs are dropped, and a named plus-one is seated in their host's party.
- Group pins: a rule line `group Kids @ 5` (also `group: Kids @ 5`) pins every guest whose group column (third column of the guest list) is Kids to table 5, for a kids' table, a head table or a family block; unknown groups and bad table numbers are reported, and the existing pin checks (table capacity, accessible tables) apply (`parseRules` in `calc.mjs`).
- `orderTable` in `calc.mjs` - seat order around each table (a ring): exhaustive up to 9 guests, greedy plus swap/reversal passes above; parties and wanted pairs end up neighbours, avoided pairs do not. Table signs, the CSV and the on-screen tables list guests in this order.
- `suggestFixes` in `calc.mjs` - for each wish the plan could not meet, the best single move or swap that raises the score within capacity, pins and accessible tables, and which other wishes it would break. Shown under "Ways to fix a missed wish"; nothing is applied.
- `compareTableCounts` in `calc.mjs` - "would one more table seat better?": re-runs the optimiser at the fewest tables that fit and up to three more, and reports wishes met and the fullest table for each; counts a pin or accessible table rules out are skipped. Nothing is applied.
- `applyMoves` in `calc.mjs` - accept a hand edit: "Apply this move" (after a check) or "Apply this fix" (on a suggested fix) re-seats those guests, refuses anything that overfills a table or breaks a pin or accessible table, re-reports the plan so the CSV, signs, floor plan and place cards all use the edited seating, and "Undo last edit" steps back. `apply-edit.check.mjs` drives it in a browser (needs a server and Playwright; see the file header).
- `checkMove` in `calc.mjs` - "what if I move Aunt Linda to table 3?": reports whether the table has room, the pin and access rules, which wishes the move would break or fix, and the score change, without applying it.
- `usage.mjs` - local-only feature counters with an opt-out.
- `how-to-make-a-wedding-seating-chart.html` - guide whose worked example is
  recomputed by the test suite.
- `how-to-handle-late-wedding-rsvps-and-drop-outs.html` - third guide (late RSVPs and drop-outs: a fresh run moves 9 of 22 returning guests, a re-seat moves 1), recomputed by the tests.
- `how-to-seat-a-kids-table-and-a-head-table-at-a-wedding.html` - fifth guide (a pinned kids table and a smaller head table via different-sized tables: list order meets 2 of 6 wishes, a search meets 6), recomputed by the tests.
- `how-to-mix-bride-and-groom-sides-at-wedding-tables.html` - sixth guide (Groups set to Spread: list order puts 8 of one side at a table, Spread puts 4 and 4 and still meets all 7 wishes), recomputed by the tests.
- `how-to-seat-a-company-dinner-or-gala-so-departments-mix.html` - seventh guide, for company dinners and galas (departments set to Spread and the host pinned: list order puts 6 of one team at a table and meets 2 of 7 wishes, Spread puts 2 of each team at every table and meets all 7), recomputed by the tests.
- `how-to-seat-divorced-parents-at-a-wedding.html` - second guide (divorced
  parents, new partners, a never-together pair), also recomputed by the tests.

## What you use today, and what this does differently

- **Paper, sticky notes or a spreadsheet:** free and private, but every "keep these two apart" and "seat these together" is checked by eye, and a late RSVP means redoing it.
- **Wedding-planning suites and seating-chart apps** (the seating tools bundled with planning sites, and standalone drag-and-drop chart makers): visual room layouts, guest-list sync and RSVP collection. They typically want an account and hold your guest list on their servers, and the table assignment is mostly drag-and-drop by you.
- **What this adds:** it searches for the assignment that meets the most of your wishes within table capacity, lists every wish it could not meet, re-seats after changes while moving as few guests as it can, and prints table signs, a find-your-table list and a caterer sheet. Your guest list never leaves the browser. It does not draw a floor plan; if you need a room layout or RSVP collection, a planning app is the better fit.

**No warranty.** Free and as-is; a planning aid, not event-planning advice or a
guarantee that any guest will be content. It lists each table's guests in order around a round table (neighbours scored by the same wishes) but does not model room layout (access needs are limited to the accessible-tables rule above), and the meal column only counts choices; it does not place guests by diet. It is a
heuristic search: tested against exhaustive search on hundreds of small random
lists, not proven optimal on large ones.

**Privacy.** Everything runs in your browser; your guest list is never uploaded.
It is remembered in this browser's local storage so you can return as RSVPs arrive ("Forget saved data" removes it), and can be saved to or loaded from a `seating-setup.json` file (`setupJson`, `parseSetup` in `calc.mjs`). Anonymous feature counts stay in local storage and can be
switched off.

MIT licence, see `LICENSE`.

how-to-handle-late-wedding-rsvps-and-dro.text:
← Event seating chart optimizer

How to handle late wedding RSVPs and drop-outs

The plan is done, the place cards are half written, and then two guests cancel and two more say yes. Re-running a seating search from scratch can shuffle a third of the room, and every moved guest is a card to reprint and a table to re-check. The better move is to re-seat: keep everyone where they are unless a change is worth it.

Open the free seating chart optimizer

The method

1. Export the current plan. Download the plan CSV (Table, Guest, ...) before you change anything.

2. Edit the guest list. Delete the drop-outs, add the new guests, and give a plus-one the same party name as their host. Remove wishes that mention people who left.

3. Paste the old CSV and re-seat. Each returning guest is tied to their old table, so they move only when the gain beats the cost. Pick low, medium or high stickiness.

4. Read the moved list. The plan names every guest who changed table, from where to where, plus who was added and who dropped.

A worked example

The sample list is 24 invented guests at 3 tables of eight, with 8 wishes (a family kept together, a never-together pair, friends who want to sit together and two pins). Joy Okafor and Carlos Mendes then drop out, and Hana and Milo Ortiz are added as one party. That leaves 22 returning guests.

ApproachReturning guests movedWishes met
Fresh optimized run9 of 227 of 7
Re-seat (medium stickiness)1 of 227 of 7

Both meet every remaining wish with eight guests at each table. The difference is that the fresh run is free to reshuffle among equally good plans, and the re-seat is not.

What the re-seat leaves out

It keeps tables, not seats within a table, and it knows only the wishes you typed. A new guest who needs step-free access, or a new feud, must be typed in as a wish. If a never-together rule or a full table forces a move, it moves, whatever the stickiness. It is a starting point for you and your planner, not a promise that every guest will be happy.

Questions

How do I update a seating chart after late RSVPs?

Paste last time's plan CSV into the late-RSVP box, update the guest list, and re-seat. Each returning guest is tied to their old table, so the optimizer moves a guest only when it gains more than the cost of moving them. Pins and never-together rules still win.

Can I keep guests from moving tables when someone drops out?

Yes. Choose high stickiness and a guest leaves their table only when a never-together rule or a full table forces it. The plan lists every guest who moved, with the old and new table, so you can tell them before the cards are printed.

What if a new guest is a plus-one of someone already seated?

Give them the same party name as their host. A party is seated together, so the new guest goes to the host's table if there is a seat, and the plan flags the party if it had to split.

Seat your own guests

Related: the general wedding seating chart guide, the divorced parents guide, the bounce house rental calculator and the container load planner.

No warranty. Free and as-is, without warranty of any kind. It is not legal, tax, financial or event-planning advice, is not a guarantee that any guest will be content with their seat, and does not replace your own judgement or your planner's. The example guests are invented and no price is stated or implied.

Independent. Not affiliated with any venue, caterer or planner, and none is named here.

Free and open source under an MIT licence. Support is entirely optional.

how-to-make-a-wedding-seating-chart.html.text:
← Event seating chart optimizer

How to make a wedding seating chart

A seating chart looks like a drawing job and is really a puzzle: dozens of small wishes, a hard limit on seats per table, and a few people who must be at a particular table. Done by hand it takes an evening of moving names around, and every fix for one wish can break another.

Open the free seating chart optimizer

The method

1. List everyone, and tag the families. Put the same party name after each member's name so they are treated as a group that wants to sit together.

2. Write the wishes as pairs. Who should sit together, who really should, who to keep apart if you can, and who must never share a table.

3. Pin the fixed seats. The couple's parents, the officiant, the head table: pin each to a table number and the search leaves them there.

4. Score and search. Every pair at the same table adds or removes points, and the plan with the best total within capacity wins. Look at the unmet wishes, decide which you can live with, and run it again for another arrangement.

A worked example

Twenty-four invented guests, three tables of eight, and eight wishes: two families (the Okafors, four people, and the Brandts, three), four pairs who should sit together, and two feuds: Uncle Ray must be kept apart from Aunt Linda and never share a table with Victor Lang. Maya Okafor and Priest Anselm are pinned to table 1, Liam Brandt to table 2.

SeatingWishes metFamilies splitScore
In the order typed4 of 8154
Optimized8 of 8081

Seating in list order puts Uncle Ray with Aunt Linda, parts Priya Nair from Tom Whitfield, Cousin Ben from Cousin Jess and Elena Petrova from Hannah Cole, and splits the Brandts across two tables. The search meets all eight wishes, keeps both families whole and keeps the pins, with eight at every table.

What the plan leaves out

It assigns tables, not seats within a table, and it knows only the wishes you typed: not who gets on, dietary needs, wheelchair access or the shape of the room. It is a starting point for you and your planner, not a promise that every guest will be happy.

Questions

How do I seat people who should not sit together?

Mark the pair with a single exclamation mark to keep them apart if possible, or two to forbid sharing a table. The optimizer treats a never-together pair as outweighing almost any friendship, so it separates them even when that splits a group of friends. If a never-together pair is still seated together, the plan lists it.

Does list order matter?

Only as a baseline. The guide's example seats the same 24 guests in the order typed, which meets 4 of 8 wishes and splits one family across two tables, and the optimizer meets all 8 with every family intact.

How many guests should sit at each table?

Round tables commonly seat 8 to 10, and a banquet table can run longer. The tool takes seats per table as an input and by default fills tables evenly, so 24 guests across 3 tables give 8 each.

Seat your own guests

how-to-mix-bride-and-groom-sides-at-wedd.text:
← Event seating chart optimizer

How to mix the bride's and groom's sides at wedding tables

Left to itself, a seating plan drifts into blocks: the bride's side at the tables near one wall, the groom's near the other, and two families who meet once a decade sit twelve feet apart. Mixing the sides is a choice, and it costs something, because people at a table are usually seated with the people they know. The optimizer lets you set how hard it pushes, and tells you what the push cost.

Open the free seating chart optimizer

The method

1. Label each guest's side. Add a third column to the guest list: Ada Okoye | | Bride side. The second column is the household or party and can stay empty. Any label works.

2. Choose Spread. In the Groups box pick Spread each group across tables (mingle). Each pair from the same group at one table now carries a small penalty, so every side is divided as evenly as the tables allow.

3. Keep your real wishes. Friends who must sit together, and anyone to keep apart. Wishes, parties and pins outweigh the mixing nudge.

4. Read "Groups by table". The report lists how many of each side sit at every table, so you can check the mix with your own eyes.

A worked example

Twenty-four invented guests at three tables of 8: twelve on the bride's side and twelve on the groom's. There are seven wishes, mostly friends within a side, plus two that cross sides (Moe Marsh with Nell Tran, and Hana Hale with Kit Marsh). No parties are entered, so the only thing the sides have in common is the label.

SeatingWishes metMost from one side at a table
In the order typed6 of 78
Ignore groups7 of 75
Spread each group7 of 74

The list typed bride's side first fills table 1 with eight people from one side and table 3 with eight from the other. A search that ignores groups meets every wish but still leaves one table with five from the same side. Spread gives each side four at every table, and still meets all seven wishes, because the nudge is weaker than a wish. In this small example mixing was free; with many same-side wishes it would not be, and the wishes would win.

What the plan leaves out

It balances head-counts by label, not personalities. Two families who dislike each other need an avoid-wish, not a group. It does not know the venue, seat positions within a table, or whether a particular mix will be comfortable for your guests. It knows only what you typed, and it is a starting point for you and your planner.

Questions

How do I stop the two sides sitting in separate blocks?

Add a third column to the guest list with each guest's side (Anya Okoye | | Bride side) and set Groups to Spread each group across tables. The search then adds a small penalty for every pair from the same group at one table, so each side is divided about evenly. Wishes still count more than the nudge, so friends you asked to sit together stay together.

Does mixing the sides break up the people I asked to sit together?

Not in the worked example: Spread still met all 7 wishes. A mixing nudge is deliberately weaker than a wish, a party or a pin, so when the two conflict, the wish wins and the report shows how the group landed. If you want a group together instead, choose Seat each group together.

Can I use groups for more than the two sides of a family?

Yes. A group is any label: Singles, Work friends, Kids, College. Spread suits groups you want to meet people (singles, colleagues), and Seat each group together suits groups that know each other. The report lists each group's head-count at every table.

Seat your own guests

how-to-seat-a-company-dinner-or-gala-so-.text:
← Event seating chart optimizer

How to seat a company dinner or gala so departments mix

Given free choice, a company dinner sorts itself by department: sales at one table, engineering at the next, and the people who never meet at work still do not meet over dinner. Mixing the teams is usually the point of the event. The optimizer lets you set how hard it pushes, keeps the host where you want them, and tells you whether your rules held.

Open the free seating chart optimizer

The method

1. Label each person's department. Add a third column to the guest list: Ana Pruitt | | Sales. The second column is the household or party and can stay empty (a plus-one goes there). Any label works.

2. Choose Spread. In the Groups box pick Spread each group across tables (mingle). Each pair from the same department at one table now carries a small penalty, so every team is divided as evenly as the tables allow.

3. Pin the host and add your real wishes. Ana Pruitt @ 1 keeps the host at table 1. Hu Tran + Nia Shaw seats two people together; Vic Hale !! Wes Nash never seats two people together. Wishes and pins outweigh the mixing nudge.

4. Read "Groups by table". The report lists how many of each department sit at every table, so you can check the mix before you print place cards.

A worked example

Twenty-four invented staff at three tables of 8: six each from Sales, Engineering, Support and Finance. There are seven wishes (six cross-team introductions and pairs, and one pair who must never share a table), plus the host pinned to table 1.

SeatingWishes metMost from one department at a table
In the order typed2 of 76
Ignore groups7 of 74
Spread each group7 of 72

The list typed department by department puts a whole team of six at one table and meets only 2 of the 7 wishes. A search that ignores groups meets every wish but leaves a table with four from one team. Spread seats exactly two from each department at every table and still meets all seven wishes, because the nudge is weaker than a wish. With many same-team wishes mixing would cost something, and the wishes would win.

What the plan leaves out

It balances head-counts by label, not seniority, personalities or who reports to whom. Use a never-together wish for a pair that must not share a table. It does not know the venue, seat positions within a table, dietary needs unless you enter meals, or whether a particular mix will feel comfortable. It knows only what you typed, and it is a starting point for you and your event team.

Questions

How do I get different departments to mix at a company dinner?

Add a third column to the guest list with each person's department (Ana Pruitt | | Sales) and set Groups to Spread each group across tables. The search penalises every pair from the same department at one table, so each department is divided about evenly. Wishes and pins count more than the nudge, so the people you asked to sit together still do.

How do I keep the CEO or the host at the head table?

Pin them with a line such as Ana Pruitt @ 1 in the wishes box. A pin is a hard rule: that person is only ever seated at that table, whatever the search would otherwise prefer.

Can I keep a manager and a direct report apart, or two people who should not share a table?

Yes. Write Vic Hale !! Wes Nash to never seat two people together; a single ! only prefers to keep them apart. The report lists every wish it could not meet, so you can see at a glance whether the rule held.

Seat your own guests

Related: the general seating chart guide, mixing two families' sides at a wedding and seating guests who need step-free access.

No warranty. Free and as-is, without warranty of any kind. how-to-seat-a-kids-table-and-a-head-tabl.text:
← Event seating chart optimizer

How to seat a kids table and a head table at a wedding

Two tables are rarely the same size as the rest: a head table for the couple and parents, and a kids table that holds every child. If you seat the room by hand, those two are fixed first and everyone else is fitted around them. The optimizer does the same, once you tell it the table sizes and pin the children.

Open the free seating chart optimizer

The method

1. Size the odd tables. In the Different-sized tables box type 1: 6, 3: 7: table 1 (the head table) gets six seats and table 3 (the kids table) seven. Every other table keeps the seats-per-table figure.

2. Pin the children. Anya Patel @ 3 seats Anya at table 3 whatever else is wished. Do the same for each child, and pin the couple and parents to the head table.

3. Add the wishes for the adults. Friends who should sit together, and any pair to keep apart. Pins win over every wish.

4. Read the report. It lists each table with its size and every wish it could not meet, and shows which parties were split.

A worked example

Twenty-four invented guests at four tables: a head table of 6, a regular table of 8, a kids table of 7 and a table of 8 (only 5 are needed). Seven children are pinned to table 3, and Maya Patel and Tom Reed are pinned to the head table with their families. There are six wishes: Maya with Gil Ward, Tom with Owen Lind, Nina Cho with Ted Moss, Hal Brandt with Vic Hale, Kay Dunn with Una Moss, and Sara Reed apart from Hal Brandt. Families are entered as parties.

SeatingWishes metParties splitScore
In the order typed2 of 6451
Optimized6 of 6463

Both honour the pins and the table sizes, so both put all seven children at table 3. The difference is the adults: the search meets all six wishes. Four families are split either way, because a child at the kids table is not at the family table. That is the price of a kids table, and the report names which families it affects so you can decide whether it is worth it.

What the plan leaves out

It assigns tables, not seats within a table. It treats the head table as a round table and does not model a long row of seats facing the room, the dance floor, or who supervises the children. It knows only the rules you typed. It is a starting point for you and your planner, not a promise that every guest will be content.

Questions

How do I put all the children at one table?

Pin each child to that table in the wishes (Anya Patel @ 3) and give the table its own size in the Different-sized tables box (3: 7), so the table has exactly the seats the children need. Pins always win, so no other wish can move a child away; the plan is rejected with a message if the table is too small for everyone pinned to it.

How do I make a head table smaller or larger than the rest?

Type its number and seats in the Different-sized tables box (1: 6 gives table 1 six seats). Every other table keeps the seats-per-table figure, and capacity checks, the search and late-RSVP re-seats all use each table's own size. The optimizer seats a head table as a round table; it does not model a long row of seats facing the room.

Will a kids table split up families?

Yes, by design: a child pinned to the kids table is no longer at their parents' table, so their party counts as split. The plan still reports it so you can see exactly which families are split, and every other wish is optimized around the pins.

how-to-seat-divorced-parents-at-a-weddin.text:
← Event seating chart optimizer

How to seat divorced parents at a wedding

Divorced parents are the classic seating problem: two people who may not want to share a table, each with a new partner, each with relatives who take a side. The way through is to decide it once, as written rules, rather than re-deciding it every time you move a name.

Open the free seating chart optimizer

The method

1. Give each side its own table. Pin each parent to a table number (Nina Castillo @ 1) so the head tables are settled before the search runs.

2. Forbid the one pairing that must not happen. Marta Reyes !! Karen Moss means never the same table. Use ! for pairs who are merely better apart.

3. Keep each parent with their partner. Put the same party name after both names, or add a + wish, and they travel together.

4. Add the friendships, then read what is left. The plan lists any wish it could not meet so you can decide which you can live with.

A worked example

Twenty-four invented guests, three tables of eight, and ten wishes. Nina and Paul Castillo (one side) are pinned to table 1, Marta and Dev Reyes to table 2, and Karen and Alan Moss to table 3. Marta Reyes must never share a table with Karen or Alan Moss, Dev Reyes is better apart from Karen, and Beth Lowe is better apart from Dana Price. Karen Moss wants to sit with Beth Lowe, Dev Reyes with Pat Quill, and four more pairs of friends and relatives want to be together.

SeatingWishes metParties splitScore
In the order typed7 of 10024
Optimized10 of 10036

List order happens to keep the former spouses apart only because the pins hold them; it still seats Beth Lowe with Dana Price and parts Karen Moss from Beth Lowe and Dev Reyes from Pat Quill. The search meets all ten wishes with eight at every table.

What the plan leaves out

It assigns tables, not seats within a table, and it knows only the wishes you typed: not who has stopped speaking to whom, custody or travel arrangements, dietary needs, wheelchair access or the shape of the room. Talk to the people involved. It is a starting point for you and your planner, not a promise that every guest will be happy.

Questions

Where should divorced parents sit at a wedding?

Give each side its own table near the front, and keep the two tables apart. Pin each parent to a table number and mark the former spouses with two exclamation marks so the optimizer will never put them at the same table, even to satisfy a friendship.

Should a divorced parent's new partner sit with them?

Usually yes: a new partner is a guest of that parent, so list them together as one party and the optimizer keeps them at the same table. Seat the new partner away from the other parent only if the people involved ask for it; the tool follows the wishes you type, not a rule about who belongs where.

What if two people are fine but not close?

Use a single exclamation mark. It tells the optimizer to keep the pair apart if it can, but lets it seat them together when the table maths needs it, and the plan lists any such pair so you can decide.

how-to-seat-wheelchair-users-and-guests-.text:
← Event seating chart optimizer

How to seat wheelchair users and guests who need step-free access at a wedding

A guest who uses a wheelchair or a walker cannot be moved to "whichever table is left". The table has to be reachable, and the plan has to keep working when you move other names around it. The way through is to write the access need down once, as a rule, so no later shuffle can break it.

Open the free seating chart optimizer

The method

1. Ask the venue which tables are step-free. Note the table numbers with a flat, wide route to the entrance, the restrooms and the food. The tool does not know the room; this is your list.

2. List them. Type the numbers in the Accessible tables box (1, 2).

3. Flag the guests. Walt Ferris @ accessible means that guest is only ever seated at a listed table. wheelchair, step-free and access work the same way.

4. Add the wishes and read what is left. Friends and family still pull toward each other, but the access rule wins. The plan names any wish it could not meet.

A worked example

Twenty-four invented guests, three tables of eight, and eight wishes. Tables 1 and 2 are step-free; table 3 is not. Walt Ferris and Gus Holt need an accessible table. Walt wants to sit with Cora Bell, Gus with Abe Lindqvist, Nell Ferris with Dot Marsh, Ines Duarte with Ravi Nair, and three more pairs of friends and relatives want to be together. Tess Brandt is better apart from Pete Voss. The Ferris, Holt and Duarte couples are each listed as a party.

SeatingWishes metParties splitScore
In the order typed4 of 8212
Optimized8 of 8039

Even the plain list-order seating honours the access rule: it places Walt and Gus at the accessible tables first, then fills the rest in the order typed, which splits two couples and misses four wishes. The search keeps Walt at table 1 and Gus at table 2, keeps every couple together, meets all eight wishes and puts eight guests at every table.

What the plan leaves out

It assigns tables, not seats within a table, and it knows only the rules you typed: not the width of the aisles, the route from the table to the restroom, hearing or vision needs, service animals, dietary needs or what each guest actually wants. Ask the guest. It is a starting point for you and your planner, not a promise that every guest will be content or that the venue is accessible.

Questions

Which tables should be accessible at a wedding?

Tables on a flat, wide route to the entrance, the restrooms and the food, with room to turn a wheelchair, and not behind a step, a dance-floor lip or a narrow gap between chairs. Only the venue can tell you which ones those are; the optimizer takes your list of table numbers and does not know the room.

How do I make sure a guest is never seated at a table they cannot reach?

Type the accessible table numbers in the Accessible tables box and add the guest to the wishes as Name @ accessible (wheelchair, step-free and access also work). That guest is only ever placed at a listed table, whatever their friends want, and the plan is rejected with a message if the listed tables are too small or a pin contradicts it.

Does the accessible rule still keep families together?

Yes. Wishes and parties still count, but the accessible rule wins when they conflict: the rest of a party is pulled to the accessible table when there is room, and the plan lists any wish it could not meet so you can decide.

index.html.text:
EVENT SEATING CHART OPTIMIZER · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

Who sits where? Let the search sort your seating chart.

Paste your guest list, add who should sit together, who to keep apart and who is pinned to a table. The optimizer assigns every guest to a table with the most wishes met, within capacity, and shows you any it could not.

A planning aid for you and your family or planner. New to this? Read how to make a wedding seating chart, with a worked example. Divorced parents or a feud? See how to seat divorced parents. Guests who use a wheelchair? See how to seat guests who need step-free access. Kids or a head table? See how to seat a kids table and a head table. Two families on opposite sides? See how to mix the bride's and groom's sides. Guests dropped out or RSVPed late? See how to re-seat without moving everyone. Planning a company dinner or gala? See how to seat it so departments mix.

1. Guests and wishes

Have the list in a spreadsheet? Paste the rows here, or . Columns named Name (or First and Last), Household or Party, Side or Group, Meal and RSVP are recognised; declined RSVPs are left out. Read in your browser, never uploaded.

A + B sit together · A ++ B really together · A ! B keep apart · A !! B never at one table · A @ 3 pin to table 3 · group Kids @ 5 pin everyone whose group (third column) is Kids to table 5

2. Tables

A head table of 12 and a kids table of 6? Write 1: 12, 5: 6 (table number, then seats). Every other table keeps the seats-per-table figure above.

Tables with step-free access (near the door, room for a wheelchair). Then add a rule line such as Grandma Rose @ accessible: she is only ever seated at one of these tables. Without a rule line this box does nothing.

Add your guests and wishes, then click Seat my guests.

Your guests, wishes and settings are remembered on this device only (browser local storage), so you can come back as RSVPs arrive.

Seating plan

Wishes it could not meet

    Ways to fix a missed wish

      Groups by table

        Meals by table

          Would a different number of tables seat better?

          What if I move someone?

          Your mother-in-law wants a different table? Check it before you touch the cards: it says whether the table has room, which wishes the move would break or fix, and the score change. Nothing changes until you press Apply, and Undo takes it back.

          3. Someone dropped out or RSVP'd late?

          Edit the guest and wish boxes above, paste the CSV you downloaded last time, and re-seat. Guests who are still coming stay at their table unless moving them is worth it, so you do not have to redo place cards or tell forty people they moved.

          How it works

          Scoring: every pair of guests that shares a table adds to a score. Members of the same party add 6, a + adds 3, a ++ adds 12, a ! takes away 6 and a !! takes away 200. The plan with the highest total wins, so a feud is separated even if it splits a friendship.

          Search: simulated annealing moves and swaps guests between tables, accepting some worse moves early so it does not get stuck, restarted six times; a hill-climbing pass then applies any move or swap that still helps. Table capacity and pinned tables are never broken. The same list gives the same plan until you ask for another arrangement. On small events the answer is checked against trying every possible arrangement.

          Seat order: each table's guests are listed in order around the table (the last seat touches the first), so a party and wanted pairs sit side by side and avoided pairs do not touch; it assumes a round table. Not modelled: a head table's row, couples at a head table sitting in a row, wheelchair access or room layout, grouping guests by dietary need (a fourth column only tallies meals for the caterer), which tables are near the stage or the door, children's tables as a row of seats (a whole group can be pinned to one table with group Kids @ 5), and how much one person dislikes another beyond the four strengths. Unverified against a real event: tested against exhaustive search on hundreds of small random lists and on a 200-guest list.

          Common questions

          How do I make a wedding seating chart?

          List every guest, mark who comes together as a party, add the pairs who must or should sit together and the pairs who should be kept apart, then fix anyone who has to be at a particular table, such as the couple or a parent. The optimizer then assigns everyone to tables so the most wishes are met within each table's capacity. You can rerun it for a different arrangement and edit by hand afterwards.

          How does the seating optimizer decide who sits where?

          Every pair of guests gets a score: parties and wanted pairs add points, avoided pairs subtract points, and a never-together pair subtracts a very large number. It searches for the assignment with the highest total, using simulated annealing followed by a hill-climbing polish, within table capacity and pinned tables. On small events its answer is checked against trying every possible arrangement.

          What do + ++ ! !! and @ mean?

          Write one rule per line. A + B means they should sit together. A ++ B means they really should. A ! B means keep them apart if you can. A !! B means never at the same table. A @ 3 pins a guest to table 3.

          Can I keep families together?

          Yes. Put the same party name after a bar on each family member's line, such as Maya Okafor | Okafor family, and the optimizer treats every pair in that party as a wish to sit together. If a party is larger than a table it says so and shows which tables it was split across.

          What if there are more guests than seats?

          The tool tells you how many seats you are short and does not produce a plan. Raise the seats per table or the number of tables. Leave the number of tables blank and it uses the fewest that fit.

          Does it spread guests evenly across tables?

          By default yes: each table is filled to about the same level so you do not end up with one packed table and one nearly empty. Untick the option to let tables fill up to their full capacity instead.

          What if a guest drops out after I have sent the seating plan?

          Edit the guest list, paste the CSV you downloaded last time into the re-seat box and click Re-seat. Guests who are still coming stay at their table unless moving them is worth it, so only a few people move and the rest of your place cards stay valid.

          Is the guest list uploaded or stored?

          It is never uploaded. Everything runs in your browser, nothing is sent to a server and there are no accounts. So you can come back as RSVPs arrive, your guest list, wishes and settings are remembered on this device only (browser local storage); click Forget saved data to remove them, or save a setup file to move to another device. Download the plan as a CSV to keep the result.

          Is the plan guaranteed to be the best possible?

          No. It is a search, so on a large event there may be a slightly better arrangement, and it only knows the wishes you typed. It is a starting point to review with your family or planner, not a substitute for judgement about people. Check the table-by-table list before printing place cards.

It is not legal, tax, financial or event-planning advice, is not a guarantee that any guest will be content with their seat, and does not replace your own judgement or your planner's. Results come from the wishes you type; real people and venues differ. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before you print place cards.

We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you enter, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record — nothing you enter is saved anywhere.

          Everything runs in your browser. Your guest list is never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (plan_run, example_loaded, report_downloaded, reseat_run, move_checked, edit_applied, table_counts_compared, signs_printed, floorplan_printed, board_printed, cards_printed, caterer_printed, guest_sheet_imported, saved_list_restored, plan_run_new_day) are counted only in local storage on your device, never with any of your data, and are switched off by Do Not Track.

render.yaml.text:
# One-click self-deploy: https://render.com/deploy?repo=<your fork URL>
# Render builds the Dockerfile in YOUR account; nothing runs on the author's.
# Starter plan on purpose: the free plan has no disk, so the published plan would vanish on restart.
# Render generates ADMIN_KEY and GUEST_TOKEN; read them in the service's Environment tab.
services:
  - type: web
    name: seating-hub
    runtime: docker
    dockerContext: ventures/event-seating-chart-optimizer
    dockerfilePath: ventures/event-seating-chart-optimizer/Dockerfile
    plan: starter
    healthCheckPath: /healthz
    disk:
      name: state
      mountPath: /data
      sizeGB: 1
    envVars:
      - key: ADMIN_KEY
        generateValue: true
      - key: GUEST_TOKEN
        generateValue: true
